topics.title: Iran Conflict
bullets: Recently, Iran’s Khamenei regime has been put under immense pressure as citizens ask for reinstatement for the old- Pahlavi rule, and secure their rights.
Security authorities ordered shutdowns to curb protests, prevent coordination, and stop images of crackdowns from reaching the outside world.
The blackout has disrupted daily life, emergency communication, and international connectivity, drawing global condemnation and human rights concerns. Iran -
Iran, officially the Islamic Republic of Iran (IRI), also known as Persia, is a country in West Asia.

It borders Turkey to the northwest and Iraq to the west, Azerbaijan, Armenia, the Caspian Sea and Turkmenistan to the north, Afghanistan to the east, Pakistan to the southeast, the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf to the south.
Iran ranks 17th globally in both geographic size and population.
It is the sixth-largest country entirely in Asia and one of the world's most mountainous countries.
Officially an Islamic republic, Iran has a Muslim-majority population.
The country is divided into five regions with 31 provinces. Tehran is the nation's capital, largest city and financial centre.
The country’s past political and economically difficulties led to the ascent of the Pahlavi line in 1925.

Their ill-planned efforts to modernize Iran resulted in widespread dissatisfaction and the dynasty's subsequent overthrow in the Islamic revolution of 1979 during the regime of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.
This revolution brought a regime to power that uniquely combined elements of a parliamentary democracy with an Islamic theocracy run by the country’s clergy.
The world’s sole Shiʿi state, Iran found itself almost immediately embroiled in a long-term war with neighboring Iraq that left it economically and socially drained.
In the last decade of the 20th century, reformists in the government opposed the conservative clergy's rule and Iran’s political and economic isolation from the international community.

However, their rise was reversed in the 21st century due to conservative leadership intervention and the increased influence of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). What is happening in Iran?
As of January 16, 2026, Iran is experiencing its ninth consecutive day of a near-total nationwide internet and telecommunications blackout.
After nearly two weeks of localized disruptions, the full-scale shutdown began on January 8, 2026.
The decision was taken by Iran’s competent security authorities, as confirmed by the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology.
Initially, the government attributed disruptions to power outages and outdated infrastructure, before acknowledging deliberate restrictions due to “prevailing circumstances.”
Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei did not announce the technical shutdown but addressed the nation on Friday, January 9, 2026.
In his address, Khamenei vowed not to retreat and described protesters as “terrorist agents” backed by foreign powers.
The blackout followed a call for mass protests by exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, prompting fears of coordinated nationwide unrest.
Iranian state media accused “terrorist agents” supported by the United States and Israel of orchestrating the violence. Why all these protests?
The protests erupting in Iran have multiple reasons behind it.
By late December 2025, point-to-point inflation exceeded 52%, while food inflation crossed 70%, making essentials like meat and cooking oil unaffordable.
Economic pressure intensified after President Masoud Pezeshkian introduced austerity measures, including ending subsidised exchange rates and raising taxes.
Wage hikes were kept well below inflation, directly triggering strikes in Tehran’s Grand Bazaar, which then spread nationwide.
Economic anger rapidly evolved into demands for the end of the Islamic Republic, reflecting a deep legitimacy crisis.
Decades of corruption, mismanagement, and the absence of credible reform convinced many Iranians that the political system is “bankrupt.”
Gen Z youth and students from universities such as Amirkabir and Shahid Beheshti joined the protests, rejecting incremental reform in favour of systemic change.
Slogans like “Neither Gaza nor Lebanon, I sacrifice my life for Iran” reflected popular rejection of ideological foreign priorities.
In June 2025, Israeli and US strikes severely damaged Iran’s nuclear infrastructure and killed senior military and scientific figures, exposing regime vulnerability.
The reimposition of UN and US sanctions in September 2025 further crippled the economy and highlighted diplomatic failure.
Statements from the Trump administration and calls for mobilisation by exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi emboldened protesters with hopes of international backing.

Chronic power blackouts, water shortages, and long-standing ethnic marginalisation—especially in Kurdish and Lur regions—turned economic despair into some of the deadliest clashes of the unrest. International reaction towards internet ban –
The international response to Iran’s nationwide internet shutdown in January 2026 has been marked by strong condemnation and fears of a potential “massacre in the dark.”
United States President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance warned Tehran that the US is “locked and loaded” if Iranian security forces continue killing peaceful protesters.
Donald Trump further cautioned Iranian leaders that they would “pay hell” if the crackdown persisted.
European Union Foreign Policy Chief Kaja Kallas condemned the shutdown as the action of a “regime afraid of its own people” and described the security response as disproportionate.
Leaders of France, Britain, and Germany (E3) issued a joint statement condemning the killing of protesters and urging respect for freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
Netherlands Justice Minister Dilan Yeşilgöz-Zegerius called for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to be designated as a terrorist organisation by the EU at the earliest.
Amnesty International described the blanket internet shutdown as a serious human rights violation in itself.
Amnesty warned that the blackout is being used to conceal grave human rights violations and crimes under international law.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi warned of a possible massacre, citing reports of hundreds of severely injured protesters reaching hospitals.
Internet monitoring group NetBlocks termed the shutdown the worst connectivity crisis in Iran’s history.
Since January 8, 2026, internet connectivity in Iran has reportedly flatlined at just 1%–5% of normal levels.

topics.title: International Solar Alliance
bullets: Recently, The US has formally withdrawn from the International Solar Alliance under President Donald Trump.
The ISA is a key global solar energy initiative co-led by India and France.
The move reflects a shift away from multilateral climate and renewable energy cooperation. International Solar Alliance (ISA)–
The ISA was conceived as a joint effort by India and France to mobilize efforts against climate change through deployment of solar energy solutions.
It was conceptualized on the sidelines of the 21st Conference of Parties (COP21) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) held in Paris in 2015.
The ISA was unveiled by PM Narendra Modi and then French President Francois Hollande on November 30, 2015.
With the amendment of its Framework Agreement in 2020, all member states of the United Nations are now eligible to join the ISA.
The ISA strives to develop and deploy cost-effective and transformational energy solutions powered by the sun.

Its aim is to help member countries develop low-carbon growth trajectories, with particular focus on delivering impact in countries categorized as Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and the Small Island Developing States (SIDS).
The ISA is guided by its ‘Towards 1000’ strategy.
This strategy aims to mobilize USD 1,000 billion of investments in solar energy solutions by 2030.
It also aims to deliver energy access to 1,000 million people using clean energy solutions and result in the installation of 1,000 GW of solar energy capacity.
This would help mitigate global solar emissions to the tune of 1,000 million tonnes of CO2 every year.
The ISA has set a target of 1 TW (terawatt) of solar energy by 2030, which current French President Emmanuel Macron said would require $1 trillion to achieve.
For meeting these goals, the ISA takes a programmatic approach.
Currently, the ISA has 9 comprehensive programmes, each focusing on a distinct application that could help scale deployment of solar energy solutions.

Activities under the programmes focuses on 3 priority areas – Analytics & Advocacy, Capacity Building, and Programmatic Support, that help create a favourable environment for solar energy investments to take root in the country. Basic facts about ISA –
The vision of the organisation is “Let us together make the sun brighter.”
While the mission is “Every home no matter how far away, will have a light at home.”
The Headquarters is in India with its Interim Secretariat being set up in Gurugram.
Ashish Khanna is the Director General of the International Solar Alliance (ISA), which is one of its kind multilateral organisation established to catalyse global solar growth.
The Director General has a term of four years and is eligible for re-election.

In 2021, the UN General Assembly granted Observer Status to the ISA, a decision India praised for fostering cooperation between the Alliance and the UN to boost global energy growth and development. Achievements of ISA –

By early 2026, the International Solar Alliance (ISA) reported significant progress toward its goals of mobilising $1 trillion in solar investments and providing clean energy access to 1 billion people by 2030.
In 2021, the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) granted the ISA Observer Status, strengthening its legitimacy and diplomatic standing in global forums.
The Global Solar Facility was established to unlock private investment, especially in Africa, through credit enhancement tools and insurance mechanisms.
The STAR-C (Solar Technology and Application Resource Centre) initiative created a network of training hubs to build technical skills and promote solar entrepreneurship.
The One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG) initiative seeks to interconnect regional and continental power grids to enable cross-border sharing of solar energy.
The SolarX Startup Challenge was launched to identify, mentor, and scale innovative solar startups in developing and emerging economies.
In late 2025, the SUNRISE Network was introduced to promote a circular economy in the solar sector, with emphasis on recycling and solar waste management.
The ISA regularly publishes analytical tools such as the “Ease of Doing Solar” report to benchmark policies and ease solar adoption. What brings this in news?

In early January 2026, US President Donald Trump officially withdrew the United States from the International Solar Alliance (ISA), signalling a major shift away from global solar and climate cooperation.
The decision was formally announced on January 7, 2026.
The withdrawal from the ISA formed part of a wider directive ordering the US exit from 66 international organisations.
These include 31 United Nations–linked entities and 35 non-UN international bodies.
Although the final order was signed in 2026, the move followed a year-long review launched soon after Trump’s inauguration in January 2025.

The withdrawal was carried out through a presidential memorandum titled “Withdrawing the United States from International Organisations, Conventions, and Treaties that are Contrary to the Interests of the United States.”
The memorandum instructed all US federal departments and agencies to take immediate steps to end participation and stop funding to the listed bodies.
The Trump administration stated that the ISA and similar bodies operate against US national interest, security, and sovereignty.
The move reflects Trump’s “America First” policy and a broader turn towards isolationism in foreign affairs.
Donald Trump asserted that his authority to withdraw stemmed from the US Constitution and existing laws, despite potential domestic legal challenges.

Despite the US exit, the India-headquartered International Solar Alliance, with 125 member and signatory countries, plans to continue its target of mobilising $1 trillion in solar investments by 2030. Impact –
The United States’ withdrawal from the International Solar Alliance (ISA) in early January 2026 is widely seen as a symbolic and strategic shift rather than an immediate operational setback.
The withdrawal could complicate the ISA’s ambition to mobilise $1 trillion in solar investments by 2030 by affecting investor confidence.
Private investors may interpret the move as reduced multilateral backing from a major global economy.
The direct financial impact remains limited, as the US paid no membership fee and a proposed $50,000 annual fee for developed countries in 2025 had not been implemented.
Indian solar industry experts believe the impact on market fundamentals will be minimal.
By late 2025, India’s solar module manufacturing capacity had reached nearly 144 GW, strengthening domestic self-reliance.
